problems: The jar is very dark. On a phone it reads as a black jar, and the red saffron threads hardly show (frames 1-12)
The pull-back from the close-up to the medium shot lurches. The framing jumps and the tabletop slides around between frames 13 and 16 instead of one smooth move
Both money bricks slide in from the right edge of the frame. His hand is on each one only once it is already in frame (rows 3-4), so the shove starts off-screen
better: Light the jar from behind or the side so the red threads glow, and hold it a little away from his glasses so it doesn't merge with the frame
Make the pull-back one eased dolly move, or hard-cut from the close-up to the medium shot
Start each brick inside the frame next to his hand so we see him grab it and push it the whole way
Push his surprise further at the end (eyebrows, lean back) and hold it a beat less: the last row is mostly the same pose

problems: The crocus is a small twisted purple shape half hidden by his hand against his chest. It barely reads as a flower on a phone (frames 1-40).
While he pulls threads, his raised hand crosses over his glasses and covers an eye several times (frames 12-13, 20-22, 29-31).
In the end pose the three threads stick straight out of his fingers and can read as red finger extensions rather than threads he is holding (frames 41-60).
better: Hold the flower lower and turned to camera with its cup open, so it reads clearly as a crocus and you can see where each thread comes from.
Keep the pulling hand to one side of his face so he never covers his own eyes.
Pinch the threads together at their bases in his fingertips, fanned at the tips, so they read as things he is holding.
The amazed hold runs about 3 seconds unchanged (frames 43-60). Add a small move, like a glance from the threads to us, or end the shot sooner.

problems: Data sits low behind the table and his hands are small and motion-blurred at his chest, so the actual pulling of threads is hard to read on a phone
The spent flowers are thrown far to the right and land in a second pile cut off by the right frame edge (rows 3-5), not in one clear pile next to him
His face barely changes the whole shot (a flat, worried look). Nothing in his acting shows the hours piling up
better: Push in or raise him so his hands and the dish are bigger in frame. The red going into the dish is the point
Toss the spent flowers onto one pile close beside him that grows in full view
Build tiredness as the window darkens: slumping shoulders, heavier blinks
Make the faster-and-faster speed-up more obvious in his hands, with the spinning clock driving it

problems: The brief asks for one big crocus close to camera, but it sits in the mid-ground on the left, smaller than Data, and ends at his feet as a small brown shape (frames 1-28).
Data is full-length and a bit far away. His face reads, but his hands and posture are small on a phone, close to the 'tiny Data' line.
The dawn lighting is dim overall. The wilted brown flower almost disappears into the dark soil (frames 13-28).
better: Move the camera low and right up to the flower, filling the lower half of the frame, with Data waist-up behind it out of focus and then sharpening as he looks up.
Put a warm rim light on the flower so the change from purple to brown pops.
Make the worried look stronger and earlier, with brows knit and his hands gripping tighter.

problems: The jar on the left pan is small and dark, so 'tiny jar of saffron' is hard to read at phone size (all frames).
His raised open hand on screen-left is partly hidden behind the beam and the jar (frames 37-54), which weakens the final gesture.
The basket is set down in front of the right pan and overlaps the scale's base and pan, cluttering the payoff picture (frames 31-54).
better: Light or enlarge the jar so its red threads read against the brass. That contrast is the whole joke.
Raise the open hand clear of the beam, above or beside it, so the 'that's what you pay for' gesture reads cleanly.
Set the basket down off to the side, away from the scale, so the level beam is unobstructed in the final frames.
Add a small settle or wobble as the beam comes level, so the levelling lands as its own moment.
